The HPTN 067/ADAPT study, conducted in Bangkok, Thailand, compared daily and non-daily PrEP dosing among men who have sex with men, as reported by Holtz et al. in 2015. The dapivirine vaginal ring, a novel HIV prevention method, has been extensively studied. Research has shown its safety, acceptability, and efficacy in reducing HIV-1 acquisition risk among women in sub-Saharan Africa. Studies such as the DREAM and HOPE trials have provided evidence supporting its use, while secondary analyses have linked greater dapivirine release to lower HIV-1 acquisition risk. The ring has also been evaluated for its impact on pregnancy outcomes, sexual experiences, and partner relationships, with findings indicating no significant adverse effects on hormonal contraception or sexual health. WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and service delivery emphasize the importance of initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) for all individuals living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 cell count. This treat-all approach has been adopted by over 120 countries, significantly scaling up ART coverage globally. Rapid ART initiation within seven days of diagnosis, or even on the same day, is recommended, particularly for individuals with advanced HIV disease. Special considerations are given to subpopulations such as pregnant and breastfeeding women, adolescents, and children. ART for pregnant women not only improves maternal health but also prevents mother-to-child transmission of HIV. For children, early ART initiation is critical, as infants and young children with HIV face high mortality rates without treatment. Recent studies have focused on the timing of ART initiation in newborns to improve outcomes and limit the viral reservoir. The WHO guidelines also address the management of advanced HIV disease, emphasizing the need for prompt ART initiation and evaluation for opportunistic infections like tuberculosis and cryptococcal meningitis.
